title: What a Sport Is
description: A sport is a physical contest in which people compete under agreed rules, aiming to score, finish first, or perform better than their rivals. The rules matter as much as the effort: they define what counts, what is forbidden, and how a winner is decided, so that strangers can compete fairly and spectators can follow the contest. Most sports combine physical skill, such as speed, strength, balance, or coordination, with mental skill, such as timing, decision-making, and teamwork. Some sports are judged, like gymnastics, some are raced against the clock, like sprinting, and some are scored by goals or points, like soccer and basketball. What unites them is structure: a beginning, a contest, and an ending that can be checked by anyone who knows the rules.

demo.code:
players = 22
print('Soccer match players on the field:', players)
print('Minutes in a regulation match:', 90)
print('Players per side:', players // 2)
demo.expected_output:
Soccer match players on the field: 22
Minutes in a regulation match: 90
Players per side: 11

history: People have played organised games for thousands of years, from running races and wrestling in ancient cultures to the codified team games of the nineteenth century.
rules: A sport is a physical contest played under agreed rules, with a defined way to score, a defined playing area or course, and officials or conventions that settle disputes.
techniques: Players learn the basic movements of their sport first, then combine them into tactics, and finally practise them under pressure so they hold up in competition.

title: The History of Sport
description: Sport is as old as play itself. Ancient peoples ran, wrestled, threw, and played ball games, and the ancient Olympic festival at Olympia brought athletes from Greek city-states together for contests that were treated as serious public events. For most of history, games varied from village to village, with local rules passed on by playing rather than by writing. That changed in the nineteenth century, when schools, clubs, and new associations wrote down common rules, formed leagues, and organised championships that let teams from different towns play each other on equal terms. The twentieth century added international federations, professional leagues, television, and the modern Olympic and Paralympic Games, turning local pastimes into worldwide contests while keeping the local club as the place where most players first learn a sport.

demo.code:

print('Ancient Olympic era begins (BCE, traditional date):', years[0])
print('First modern Olympic Games:', years[1])
print('First Paralympic Games:', years[2])
print('Years between modern Olympics and first Paralympics:', years[2]-years[1])

history: Ancient Olympic games were held at Olympia in Greece, and ball games, wrestling, and running contests appear in many early civilisations on every continent.
competitions: Modern sport took its present form when clubs, national associations, and international federations wrote common rules and organised regular championships.
statistics: No single date marks the birth of sport; instead, each sport has its own documented codification date, and this record gives those dates only where the sport's own federation records them.

title: The Olympic Movement
description: The Olympic Movement is the worldwide organisation behind the Olympic Games, built on the idea that athletes from every country should meet in peaceful competition under shared rules. The modern Games began in Athens in 1896 and are now held every four years in summer and winter editions, with a host city preparing venues, housing, and transport for thousands of athletes. The International Olympic Committee oversees the movement, while each sport's international federation runs its own events and sets its technical rules. The Olympic motto, faster, higher, stronger, together, captures the aim: personal bests pursued in a spirit that respects rivals. The Games also carry ceremonies, a torch relay, and an athletes' village, all designed to make the meeting of nations visible as well as competitive.

print('Olympic cycle in years:', cycle)
print('Summer and winter editions per cycle:', 2)
print('Games in 20 years at full cycle:', 20 // cycle)
demo.expected_output:
Olympic cycle in years: 4

history: The modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896, revived by Pierre de Coubertin, and have since been held every four years except when cancelled by world wars.
competitions: The Games bring together athletes in summer and winter editions, with host cities chosen years in advance and sports added or removed by the International Olympic Committee.
rules: Olympic competition follows each sport federation's rules, with eligibility, anti-doping, and fair-play rules applying across all sports.

title: The Paralympic Movement
description: The Paralympic Movement organises elite sport for athletes with impairments, and its Games now run in the same host cities as the Olympic Games, shortly after them. It began with the Stoke Mandeville Games in 1948, organised for athletes with spinal cord injuries, and grew into the first Paralympic Games in Rome in 1960. Paralympic sport covers a wide range: wheelchair racing, sitting volleyball, goalball for athletes with vision impairment, para swimming, para athletics, and many more. Because impairments differ, athletes are classified into groups so that competition is between athletes of similar function, and equipment such as racing wheelchairs, prosthetic blades, and tandem cycles is regulated to keep the contest fair. The movement's point is plain: impairment changes how an athlete competes, not whether they can compete at the highest level.

history: The Paralympic Games grew from the Stoke Mandeville Games for athletes with spinal injuries, first held in 1948, and became a parallel Games movement in 1960 in Rome.
rules: Paralympic athletes are classified by impairment so that competition is fair between athletes with similar functional ability.
safety: Classification, adapted equipment, and trained guides and pilots let athletes with a wide range of impairments compete safely at elite level.

title: How Sport Is Governed
description: Sport is governed in layers. At the top, an international federation writes the rules of its sport, organises world championships, and admits national federations as members. Below it, national federations run domestic leagues, cups, coaching qualifications, and national teams, and regional associations handle local fixtures and referees. Clubs sit at the base: they own or rent grounds, employ coaches, register players, and give beginners their first matches. The layers check each other: federations cannot change the laws of a game without consulting the people who play and officiate it, and clubs cannot invent their own scoring system and expect other clubs to accept the result. Good governance also covers money, safeguarding of young players, and discipline, so that a dispute on the field has a clear route to a fair decision off it.

demo.code:
levels = ['club', 'regional', 'national federation', 'international federation']
for i, level in enumerate(levels, 1):
    print(i, level)
print('Governance layers:', len(levels))
demo.expected_output:
1 club
2 regional
3 national federation
4 international federation

rules: Each sport has an international federation that writes its rules, while national federations run domestic leagues and select national teams, and clubs are where most players belong.
competitions: Leagues, cups, and championships are organised in pyramids, so a local club can in principle rise through promotion to the top division.
history: Governing bodies grew from nineteenth-century associations that codified rules so that matches between strangers could be played fairly.

title: Amateur and Professional Sport
description: Amateur and professional sport differ mainly in how players are paid and how much time they can give to training. An amateur plays for enjoyment, fitness, or pride, usually unpaid, and fits sport around work or study. A professional is paid to play, trains full-time, and is employed by a club or supported by sponsorship and prize money. For much of the nineteenth century, many sports restricted professionalism, arguing that pay would corrupt fair play, but crowds wanted to watch the best, and the best needed to train full-time to reach that standard. Today most major sports accept both: professional leagues at the top, amateur leagues below, and pathways between them, with rules about eligibility so that a player moving between levels does so fairly.

print('Amateur training hours per week (example):', amateur_hours)
print('Professional training hours per week (example):', pro_hours)

history: Early modern sport prized the amateur, who played for love of the game, while professional sport grew as crowds paid to watch the best players and clubs paid them to play.
competitions: Professional leagues sell tickets and broadcast rights and pay players, while amateur competitions rely on volunteers, membership fees, and grants.
training: Professionals train full-time with coaches, analysts, and medical staff; amateurs fit training around work or study.

title: Youth Sport
description: Youth sport is where most athletes begin, and its purpose is broader than finding future champions. Children learn to run, jump, throw, catch, and balance, and they learn to take turns, follow rules, lose gracefully, and work as a team. Good youth coaching keeps sessions short, fun, and full of activity, uses smaller fields, balls, and goals suited to children's size, and gives every child playing time rather than benching the slowest. Competition is introduced gradually, with results mattering less than improvement at younger ages, and safeguarding rules require qualified coaches, background checks, and clear behaviour standards for adults. When youth sport works, children stay active for life, whether or not they ever reach an elite team.

print('Minutes per child if shared equally:', minutes // players)
print('Small-sided games raise touches per child')

training: Youth coaching emphasises fun, basic movement, and small-sided games, with competition introduced gradually as children grow.
safety: Safeguarding, qualified coaches, age-group rules, and appropriate equipment sizes protect young players.
techniques: Children learn best by playing: short practices, many touches of the ball, and games that let every child take part.

title: Women in Sport
description: Women's sport has grown from exclusion to a central place in world sport, but the history matters for understanding the present. Women were barred from many early competitions, including most events at the first modern Olympic Games, and had to build their own clubs, leagues, and championships. Through the twentieth century, campaigners won entry to more events, and laws and policies in several countries required equal access to school and university sport. Today women's leagues and championships run in most major sports, professional women's soccer and basketball draw large crowds, and women's events are a major part of the Olympic and Paralympic programmes. Gaps remain in pay, prize money, and media coverage in many sports, and closing them is now a central task for governing bodies.

history: Women were long excluded from many competitions, including early Olympic events, and fought for entry, funding, and media coverage through the twentieth century.
competitions: Women's leagues, cups, and championships now run in most major sports, with professional women's leagues growing in soccer, basketball, cricket, and tennis.
statistics: Participation and audience figures for women's sport have grown sharply in recent years, though pay and coverage gaps remain in many sports.

title: Sport and Health
description: Sport is one of the most reliable ways to stay healthy, because it combines movement with enjoyment and social contact, which makes people keep doing it. Regular play strengthens the heart and lungs, builds muscle and bone, improves balance and coordination, and helps control weight. It also supports mental health: a regular fixture gives routine, teammates give social support, and progress gives a sense of achievement. The benefits depend on sensible practice: warm up, increase load gradually, rest between hard sessions, and seek advice early for pain that does not settle. Sport is not risk-free, but for most people the health risks of inactivity are larger than the risks of well-coached, well-equipped play.

training: Regular sport improves heart and lung fitness, strength, flexibility, balance, and coordination, and supports mental health through routine, social contact, and achievement.
safety: Health benefits depend on sensible loading: warm-ups, gradual progression, rest days, and early attention to pain or injury.
statistics: Health guidance in many countries recommends regular moderate activity for adults and children, with sport one of the most enjoyable ways to reach it.

title: Sport Science
description: Sport science applies measurement to training. Scientists and analysts track how fast an athlete runs, how much force they produce, how their heart rate responds to effort, and how quickly they recover, and coaches use those numbers to set training loads, plan rest, and choose tactics. Video analysis breaks a skill into frames so a coach can show an athlete exactly where a movement goes wrong, and wearable devices record distance, speed, and impacts during matches. Nutrition, sleep, and psychology are part of the same science: fuel, rest, and mindset all change performance measurably. The aim is not to replace coaching judgement with numbers, but to give judgement better evidence, so that training is planned rather than guessed.

demo.code:
distance_m = 5000
time_s = 900
print('Distance (m):', distance_m)
print('Time (s):', time_s)
print('Average speed (m/s):', round(distance_m / time_s, 2))

training: Sport scientists measure speed, power, endurance, and recovery, and use the numbers to plan training loads and rest.
techniques: Video analysis, wearable trackers, and force plates let coaches see what the eye misses and correct technique precisely.
safety: Load monitoring and screening help spot fatigue and injury risk before a small problem becomes a season-ending one.

title: Coaching
description: Coaching is the work of helping athletes improve, and it is a skill in its own right, separate from playing ability. A coach plans the season, breaks a sport into teachable skills, designs practices that give every athlete repetitions, and watches for errors to correct with short, specific feedback. Good coaches also manage people: they set expectations, handle selection fairly, keep parents and players informed, and build a team culture where effort is praised and mistakes are treated as part of learning. Qualifications now exist in most sports, from beginner courses for volunteers to elite diplomas for professional coaches, and safeguarding training is a standard part of them. The best coaches are judged not only by wins, but by whether their athletes improve, enjoy the sport, and stay in it.

print('Athletes:', athletes)

training: Coaches plan seasons, design practices, teach skills step by step, and give feedback that athletes can act on.
techniques: Good coaching mixes demonstration, short clear instructions, guided practice, and questions that make athletes think for themselves.
history: Coaching qualifications now run in most sports, with levels from beginner helper to elite performance coach.

title: Officiating and Fair Play
description: Officiating is what makes fair play enforceable. Referees, umpires, and judges apply the rules neutrally, keep time, record the score, and decide incidents that players dispute, and their decisions stand unless a sport's review system overturns them. Officials train in the rules, in positioning so they can see the play, in clear signals so players and spectators understand decisions, and in staying calm under pressure from crowds and players. Fair play is the wider ethic behind officiating: respect for opponents, honesty about fouls, acceptance of decisions, and refusal to cheat, dive, or abuse officials. Video review assists officials in some sports, but it does not replace them, because judgement about intent and advantage still needs a human on the spot.

print('Decisions in a match (example):', decisions)
print('Correct:', correct)
print('Accuracy:', round(correct / decisions * 100, 1), '%')
demo.expected_output:

Correct: 38

rules: Referees, umpires, and judges enforce the rules, keep time, record scores, and decide contested incidents, with video review assisting in some sports.
history: Officiating grew with codified sport: once rules were written, someone had to apply them neutrally, and training and assessment followed.
techniques: Officials train in positioning, signalling, communication, and decision-making under pressure, and are assessed after matches.

title: Ethics in Sport
description: Ethics in sport asks a simple question: what does it mean to compete well, not merely to win? The answer covers honesty, respect for opponents and officials, inclusion regardless of background, and the duty of coaches and administrators to protect young players. Cheating, whether by breaking a rule, faking an injury to deceive an official, or fixing a result for money, breaks the shared trust that makes competition meaningful: if results can be bought, no result means anything. Ethical sport also covers wider duties, such as honest reporting of age and eligibility, fair treatment of all participants, and care for the environment at events. Governing bodies publish codes of conduct and run disciplinary systems, but ethics ultimately live in everyday decisions by players, coaches, and officials.

print('Cheating breaks shared trust in results')
print('Fair play applies to players, coaches, officials, and crowds')
demo.expected_output:
Ethical tests: honesty, respect, inclusion, protection
Cheating breaks shared trust in results

rules: Sporting ethics cover honesty, respect, inclusion, and the duty of adults to protect young and vulnerable participants.
history: Ethical codes grew as sport professionalised and money and media pressure created new temptations to cheat or fix results.
competitions: Match-fixing, bribery, and deliberately losing are banned in every major sport and can end careers and bring criminal penalties in some countries.

title: Doping and Anti-Doping
description: Doping means using banned substances or methods to gain an unfair performance advantage, and anti-doping is the system built to stop it. The World Anti-Doping Agency publishes a list of prohibited substances and methods, updated yearly, and athletes can be tested in competition and out of competition, with samples stored for later retesting as science improves. Violations bring suspensions, loss of results and prize money, and, in some cases, lifetime bans. The rules matter for two reasons: fairness, because doping lets one athlete buy an advantage others refuse, and health, because many banned substances damage the heart, liver, hormones, and mental health. Athletes are also responsible for what is in their bodies, which is why they check medicines and supplements carefully against the prohibited list.

positives = 12
print('Tests (example):', tests)
print('Positive results (example):', positives)
print('Positive rate:', round(positives / tests * 100, 2), '%')

rules: Doping is the use of banned substances or methods to improve performance, and anti-doping rules ban them, test athletes, and punish violations.
safety: Many banned substances carry serious health risks, including heart, liver, and hormonal damage, which is one reason they are banned.
history: Modern anti-doping began with testing at major Games and grew into the World Anti-Doping Agency and a global code adopted by federations.

title: Sport Media and Broadcasting
description: Sport media and broadcasting turn a match into an event that millions can follow. Newspapers and radio came first, giving results and live commentary to people who could not attend, and television then added pictures, slow-motion replay, and expert analysis that let viewers see tactics they would miss from the stands. Streaming has since added choice: viewers can watch on phones, choose camera angles, and follow statistics live. Broadcast rights are now a major source of money for professional sport, funding player wages, club facilities, and grassroots programmes in some leagues, but they also shape schedules, with matches moved to suit audiences. Good coverage explains the sport as well as showing it, so that a new viewer can understand why a decision or tactic mattered.

history: Sport broadcasting grew from newspaper reports and radio commentary to television and streaming, turning local matches into worldwide events.
competitions: Broadcast rights fund much of professional sport, with leagues selling rights and using the income to pay players, clubs, and facilities.
techniques: Modern coverage uses multiple cameras, slow-motion replay, graphics, and expert commentary to explain tactics to viewers.

title: The Suite Map: How All Sports Databases Connect
description: This record maps the whole sports suite. The flagship pair, sports, explains what sport is, its history, its Olympic and Paralympic movements, its governance, and its science and ethics. Around it sit the family pairs: team-sports covers volleyball, handball, netball, and other team games; soccer-football covers the world's most played team game in depth; basketball covers its own rules, skills, and competitions; and later pairs cover American football, cricket, tennis, individual sports, combat sports, water sports, winter sports, racquet sports, motorsport, athletics, gymnastics, and esports disciplines. Named cousins are cross-linked, never rebuilt: sports-teams, sports-recreation, sports-stats, olympics, olympic-history, famous-athletes, and basketball-plays. Together the sixteen Wave 1 pairs hold 512 records, two editions of 16 for each pair, and every record is a full file with a working demo.

history: This suite begins with the flagship sports pair and branches into team, soccer, basketball, and later pairs covering every major sport family.
competitions: Each pair holds 16 records in two editions, and the suite as a whole marches toward a million records across its databases.
rules: Records cross-link rather than duplicate: a sport covered by its own pair is linked from other pairs, never rebuilt as a record there.
